extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of spherical trigonometry (mathematics/astronomy/navigation)
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter presenting definitions, propositions, corollaries and solution rules for spherical triangles (including right-angled cases and Napier's rules) used to solve spherical-trigonometry problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition I — Pole of a circle on a sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The pole of a circle of the sphere is a point on the superficies of the sphere from which all straight lines drawn to the circumference of the circle are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to define special points (poles) associated to great circles; appears repeatedly in constructions and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition II — Great circle
rubrics_metrics.description: A great circle of the sphere is any circle whose plane passes through the centre of the sphere, and whose centre therefore is the same with that of the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental object: sides of spherical triangles are arcs of great circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III — Spherical triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: A spherical triangle is a figure upon the superficies of a sphere comprehended by three arches of three great circles, each of which is less than a semicircle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the domain for all subsequent propositions: triangles formed by arcs of great circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition IV — Spherical angle
rubrics_metrics.description: A spherical angle is that which on the superficies of a sphere is contained by two arches of great circles, and is the same with the inclination of the planes of these great circles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates surface angles to dihedral (plane) angles between planes of great circles; used to interpret and compute spherical angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. I — Great circles bisect one another
rubrics_metrics.description: Great circles which have a common centre have a common section that is a diameter of each and which bisects them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple geometric fact used in many constructions; proof: common centre implies common central diameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. II — Arch from pole to circumference is a quadrant
rubrics_metrics.description: The arch of a great circle between the pole and the circumference of another is a quadrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If D is the pole of great circle ABC and a great circle through D meets ABC in C, then DC is a quadrant (i.e., a quarter-circle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III — Measure of spherical angle equals arc between poles
rubrics_metrics.description: If a great circle described meets two great circles AB, AC (passing through its pole A) in B, C, the angle at the centre of the sphere upon the circumference BC is the same with the spherical angle BAC, and the arch BC is called the measure of the spherical angle BAC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates measure of a spherical angle to the central angle subtended by the opposite arc; corollary: two quadrants from a point produce a great circle whose pole is that point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IV — Base angles equal in isosceles spherical triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: In isosceles spherical triangles the angles at the base are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to plane geometry: if two sides (arcs) are equal, base angles are equal. Proof uses symmetry about centre and right-angle constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. V — Converse: equal angles imply equal opposite sides
rubrics_metrics.description: If in a spherical triangle two of the angles are equal, the sides opposite to them are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Converse of Prop. IV; proof mirrors IV using same constructions in reverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VI — Any two sides exceed the third
rubrics_metrics.description: Any two sides of a spherical triangle are greater than the third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from the corresponding property of the three plane angles at the centre of the sphere: any two of those plane angles exceed the third.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VII — Sum of three sides less than a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: The three sides of a spherical triangle together are less than a circle (i.e., less than 360°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows because the three plane angles at the centre are less than four right angles, so the total arcs are less than four quadrants (a circle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VIII — Greater angle opposite greater side
rubrics_metrics.description: In a spherical triangle the greater angle is opposite the greater side; conversely the greater side is opposite the greater angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs auxiliary equal-angle point to compare corresponding sides, similar in spirit to plane geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IX — Relation of sum of two sides to base angles (internal vs external)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the sum of two sides AB and BC is greater than, equal to, or less than a semicircle, then the internal angle at the base AC is greater than, equal to, or less than the external and opposite angle BCD; equivalently the sum of A and ACB is greater than, equal to, or less than two right angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides criterion comparing side-sums to semicircle and deducing inequalities between internal and external opposite angles; includes three cases with geometric construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. X — Supplemental triangle via poles; supplements relations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the angular points A, B, C of spherical triangle ABC are the poles of three great circles, these great circles intersect to form a supplemental triangle FDE whose sides are supplements of the measures of opposite angles of ABC, and whose angles are supplements of the sides of ABC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes duality between sides and angles via pole construction; used to transform angle-measure problems to side-measure problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XI — Three angles bounds: greater than 2 right angles, less than 6 right angles
rubrics_metrics.description: The three internal angles of a spherical triangle are greater than two right angles in total and less than six right angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses relationship with supplemental triangle and bounds on its sides to bound sum of angles; gives global constraint on angle sums in spherical triangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XII — Ordering of arcs from a point
rubrics_metrics.description: From any point C (not the pole) arcs CA, CD, CE, CF, etc., drawn to a great circle, the greatest is the one passing through the pole of that circle (CA), and the smallest is the one to the point opposite; arcs nearer to CA are greater than those more remote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides monotonic ordering of arcs from a fixed point; proof reduces to comparing straight-line chords in perpendicular plane sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIII — In right-angled spherical triangle sides and opposite angles 'same affection'
rubrics_metrics.description: In a right-angled spherical triangle the sides are of the same 'affection' (i.e., being greater or less than a quadrant) as their opposite angles (being greater or less than a right angle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives categorical relation: if a side < quadrant then opposite angle < right angle, etc.; proven by constructing quadrants and comparing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIV — Hypothenuse quadrant relation from sides' affection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the two sides about the right angle are of the same affection (both < quadrant or both > quadrant), the hypothenuse is less than a quadrant; if they are of different affection, the hypothenuse is greater than a quadrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes cases and uses pole/quadrant constructions to compare hypothenuse length to quadrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XV — Converse of Prop. XIV
rubrics_metrics.description: If the hypothenuse of a right-angled triangle is greater or less than a quadrant, then the two sides about the right angle are of different or the same affection respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct converse demonstrated similarly to Prop. XIV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XVI — Perpendicular from vertex determines base-angles' affection
rubrics_metrics.description: In any spherical triangle ABC, if the perpendicular AD from A upon base BC falls within the triangle, then base angles B and C are of the same affection; if the perpendicular falls outside the triangle, the base angles are of different affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary: position of foot of perpendicular (inside/outside) gives criterion for whether base angles are both > or both < right angles (or mixed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XVII — Sine–tangent relation in right-angled spherical triangles
rubrics_metrics.description: In right-angled spherical triangles the sine of either side about the right angle is to the radius as the tangent of the remaining side is to the tangent of the angle opposite that remaining side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructs perpendiculars to relate rectilinear sines/tangents to spherical arcs; corollary: given two of the two sides and the opposite angle, the third is determined; also relates sine to cotangent of adjacent angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XVIII — Sine relation: hypothenuse, side, and opposite angle
rubrics_metrics.description: In right-angled spherical triangles the sine of the hypothenuse is to the radius as the sine of either side is to the sine of the angle opposite that side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analog of plane right-triangle sine rule; corollary: of hypotenuse, a side, and its opposite angle, any two determine the third.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIX — Cosine–cotangent–tangent relation
rubrics_metrics.description: In right-angled spherical triangles the co-sine of the hypothenuse is to the radius as the co-tangent of either of the angles is to the tangent of the remaining angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by complementary-triangle construction (introducing complements) and invoking Prop. XVII; gives relations among complements enabling various solution formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XX — Cosine of angle relates tangents of adjacent side and hypothenuse
rubrics_metrics.description: In right-angled spherical triangles the co-sine of an angle is to the radius as the tangent of the side adjacent to that angle is to the tangent of the hypothenuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from complementary-triangle constructions and Prop. XVII; used to convert between angle cosines and arc tangents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXI — Cosine of side relation (hypothenuse and other side)
rubrics_metrics.description: In right-angled spherical triangles the co-sine of either of the sides is to the radius as the co-sine of the hypothenuse is to the co-sine of the other side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives ratio relations among cosines of sides and hypothenuse; useful for solving right-angled cases using cosine relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXII — Cosine of side to radius equals cosine of opposite angle to sine of other angle
rubrics_metrics.description: In right-angled spherical triangles the co-sine of either of the sides is to the radius as the co-sine of the angle opposite to that side is to the sine of the other angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another variant linking cosines of sides with trigonometric functions of angles; useful in deriving Napier's rules and table solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/Concept — Circular parts of a right-angled spherical triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: The circular parts of a right-angled spherical triangle are: the complement of the hypothenuse, the complements of the angles, and the two (other) sides — five parts arranged in circular order. Any three taken are either contiguous (middle part with two adjacent extremes) or non-contiguous (middle part with two opposite extremes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces the five-part circular ordering used in Napier's rules; defines terminology 'middle part', 'adjacent extremes', 'opposite extremes'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Napier's Rule I (for circular parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rectangle contained by the radius and the sine of the middle part is equal to the rectangle contained by the tangents of the adjacent parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of Baron Napier's two mnemonic rules to solve right-angled spherical triangles; demonstrated by combining previously proved propositions (notably 17–22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Napier's Rule II (for circular parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rectangle contained by the radius and the sine of the middle part is equal to the rectangle contained by the co-sines of the opposite parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complementary Napier rule equivalent to Rule I; both yield the set of identities used to solve all right-triangle cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: General proposition — Solution of right-angled spherical triangle from any two parts
rubrics_metrics.description: In a right-angled spherical triangle, of the three sides and three angles, any two being given (besides the right angle), the other three may be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement underpinning the table of sixteen cases: from any pair of known parts one can derive the rest using the propositions and Napier's rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table — Sixteen cases of right-angled spherical triangles (solution recipes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete table enumerating 16 possible combinations of two given parts (sides/angles) for right-angled spherical triangle and stating which formulas (from Props. 17–22, Napier's rules, or corollaries) to use to find the unknowns; includes case-by-case notes about the 'affection' (greater/less than quadrant) and ambiguous cases (cases 2, 8, 13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recipe sheet: for each case the text specifies which ratio or identity to use (e.g., R : Co-S AC :: b, C : Co-S B) and extra logical checks about quadrant/angle-affection to resolve ambiguities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity note — Certain cases admit two solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The second, eighth, and thirteenth cases are called ambiguous and admit two solutions because it is not determined whether the side or the sought angle is greater or less than a quadrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical warning: numerical or contextual information is needed to resolve the ambiguous cases when solving from given data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXIII — Sine rule for spherical triangles
rubrics_metrics.description: In spherical triangles (right-angled or oblique) the sines of the sides are proportional to the sines of the angles opposite them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General spherical sine law: sin(AB) : sin(BC) : sin(CA) = sin(A) : sin(B) : sin(C). Proof reduces oblique case to right-angled decomposition and applies Prop. XVIII repeatedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXIV — (begins) further relations for spherical triangles
rubrics_metrics.description: Text begins Prop. XXIV following the sine rule (full statement not present in this chunk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuation likely contains additional cosine rules or formulae for oblique spherical triangles (not fully present in this excerpt).
